  That November, the automated beacon went in on the far headland. The letter came in a government envelope, thin and polite. The station
  would be decommissioned at the end of the month. Marguerite read it twice at the kitchen table, then folded it into quarters and put it in
  the drawer where she kept birthday cards and the tide tables.

  She didn't tell anyone at first. Her nephew Daniel called on Sundays from Halifax and asked whether the wind was still bad out there. She
  said it was fine. The gulls had stopped nesting on the rocks below, and the fog horn had been silent since spring, but the lamp still
  turned, and that was what mattered.

  On the first Tuesday of December, a storm came in from the northeast. It was the kind of storm the old keepers wrote about in their
  logbooks, with waves that broke over the lower rail and a wind that found every gap in the stone. Marguerite made her rounds at dusk as
  always. At the top, she lit the lamp, and the beam swept out over the black water.

  Halfway through the night, she saw a light answer it. Small and yellow, bobbing in the trough between swells, it was a fishing boat, and
  it was turning toward the rocks. She picked up the radio and called the number that was still painted on the door. A young voice answered,
  thick with fear. The engine had died. They were drifting.

  "Keep your eyes on the light," she told him. "Don't look at the waves. Look at the light."

  She talked him through the hours. She told him about the gannets that dived off the point in summer, the way the seals hauled themselves
  onto the ledge at low tide, the name of every rock. When his voice steadied, she asked him his name. Teodor, he said. He was nineteen. His
  father had taken the boat out alone that morning and had not come back, and Teodor had gone looking for him.

  Near dawn, the sea settled. A coast guard cutter came around the point with its searchlight hunting the water. Teodor was found clinging
  to a shattered oar, cold and coughing but alive, and his father's body was recovered by noon.

  When the storm passed, Marguerite climbed the ninety-six steps one last time. The fourth rang high, and the fifty-first creaked under her
  weight. At the top, she stood beside the lens and watched the grey light spread over the bay.

  The next morning, she took the government letter from the drawer and wrote a reply. She asked whether the station could remain staffed
  through the spring, for the fishermen, in case of another storm. She didn't expect the answer to be yes. But she signed her name in the
  careful hand her mother had taught her, and she posted it before she could change her mind.

  Then she went back up the steps.

  pear
